```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(scTreeSim)
library(ggtree)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
source("helpers.R")  # plotting helpers of the vignettes: plot_tree(), plot_alleles(), ...
```

`sim_gt16_nt_diploid()` evolves diploid single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) along a fixed tree under the
GT16 model of CellPhy (Kozlov et al., 2022), with the sequencing error model of phylonco (Chen et al., 2022).
Every site carries a **genotype** of two nucleotides, one per allele. Genotypes are phased: the 16 states are
the ordered pairs `AA, AC, ..., TT`, so `AC` and `CA` are different states. A simulation has three parts:

| part | what it does | arguments / functions |
|---|---|---|
| substitution model | how a genotype changes along a distance | `rates`, `pi`, `origin_seq` or `n_sites` |
| clock model | how much distance each branch gets | `clock_strict()`, `clock_relaxed()`, `spike()` |
| tip error | what is observed at the tips | `epsilon` (amplification and sequencing error), `delta` (allelic dropout) |

The clock models are the same as for `sim_binary()` (see `vignette("simulate_binary")`). The output is
a list of two tables with one row per node, the true genotypes (`true`) and the genotypes after the error
model (`observed`), either as strings of genotypes separated by `_` (`format = "genotype"`, default) or as
two aligned allele sequences (`format = "alleles"`).

All simulations below use 40 sites on the multi-type tree of `vignette("simulate_barcodes")`. The heatmaps
show the genotypes of the tips with **two rows per cell**: allele 1 above, allele 2 below, one colour per
nucleotide. A site is heterozygous where the two rows of a cell differ.

```{r tree}
origin_time <- 3.6
ntype <- 2
shape <- c(100, 1)
scale <- 1 / shape
r <- 0.11
Xi_as <- matrix(c(0.0, 0.0, r, 0.0), nrow = ntype, ncol = ntype)
Xi_s  <- matrix(c(1 - r, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0), nrow = ntype, ncol = ntype)

set.seed(23)
tree <- sim_adb_origin_samp(origin_time, scale, shape, death_prob = c(0.1, 0.1),
                            sampling_prob = 0.8, origin_type = 0,
                            asym_trans_prob = Xi_as, sym_trans_prob = Xi_s, collapse = FALSE)
stopifnot(!is.null(tree))  # a simulation with too few tips returns NULL: try another seed

plot_tree(tree, color = "type", show_nodes = TRUE)
```

# The GT16 model

A substitution changes **one allele at a time**: `AG` can become `CG`, `GG`, `TG` (first allele) or `AA`,
`AC`, `AT` (second allele), but not `CT` in a single step. The rate from genotype `xy` to `x'y` is the
exchangeability of the two nucleotides that change (`rates`, in the order AC, AG, AT, CG, CT, GT) times the
equilibrium frequency of the new genotype (`pi`). `pi` is given either for the 16 genotypes or for the four
nucleotides, in which case the genotype frequencies are the products, e.g. `pi_AG = pi_A * pi_G`.

The rate matrix is scaled to one expected substitution per genotype site per unit of distance, where a
change of either allele counts. A distance `d` therefore gives about `d / 2` substitutions per allele.

# Two alleles from a homozygous origin

To follow the two alleles, we start every site homozygous: the origin genotype is given as two aligned
allele sequences (`origin_seq`), here twice the same random sequence. With a strict clock of 0.15 expected
substitutions per genotype site per unit of time:

```{r strict}
set.seed(1)
origin <- paste(sample(c("A", "C", "G", "T"), 40, replace = TRUE), collapse = "")
snv <- sim_gt16_nt_diploid(tree, origin_seq = c(origin, origin), clock = clock_strict(0.15))
names(snv)
substr(head(snv$true, 3)$genotype, 1, 32)  # the first 11 sites of the first three nodes
```

With `format = "alleles"`, the same simulation is returned as the two allele sequences of every node, the
same form as `origin_seq`, so that a node can be the origin of another simulation:

```{r alleles}
set.seed(1)
snv_alleles <- sim_gt16_nt_diploid(tree, origin_seq = c(origin, origin), clock = clock_strict(0.15),
                                   format = "alleles")
substr(head(snv_alleles$true, 3)$allele_1, 1, 11)
substr(head(snv_alleles$true, 3)$allele_2, 1, 11)
```

```{r strict-plot}
plot_alleles(tree, snv)
```

The two alleles of a cell evolve independently, so most substitutions make a homozygous site
heterozygous (the two rows of a cell differ), and these are shared by related cells. A site turns into
another homozygous genotype only if both alleles change.

`rates` and `pi` set which substitutions are likely. Without `origin_seq`, the origin is drawn from the
equilibrium `pi` (`n_sites` = number of sites). Here transitions (A <-> G, C <-> T) are four times as fast as
transversions, and A and T are more frequent than C and G:

```{r rates-pi}
set.seed(2)
snv_at <- sim_gt16_nt_diploid(tree, n_sites = 40, rates = c(1, 4, 1, 1, 4, 1), pi = c(0.3, 0.2, 0.2, 0.3),
                              clock = clock_strict(0.15))
tips <- snv_at$true$node %in% seq_along(tree@phylo$tip.label)
round(prop.table(table(unlist(strsplit(gsub("_", "", snv_at$true$genotype[tips]), "")))), 2)
plot_alleles(tree, snv_at)
```

# Clock models

As for binary sequences, a clock model gives every branch, including the root edge, a distance
(`clock_strict()`, `clock_relaxed()`), optionally with spikes at cell divisions (`spike()`). One clock
draw is shared by all sites. `clock_tree()` stores the draw in the tree, and `clock = NULL` simulates on it,
so that the genotypes can be plotted next to the distance tree.

The mean of a spike is in expected substitutions per genotype site, so `spike(mean = m / n_sites)` gives
about `m` substitutions over all sites at a division. Here, a relaxed clock and a strict clock with spikes
of 2 substitutions over the 40 sites (three times as much after divisions of type 1 cells):

```{r clocks, fig.height = 9}
set.seed(3)
ct_relaxed <- clock_tree(tree, clock_relaxed(0.15, sd = 1))
ct_spike <- clock_tree(tree, clock_strict(0.05, spike = spike(2 / 40, shape = 2, by_type = c(1, 3))))
snv_relaxed <- sim_gt16_nt_diploid(ct_relaxed, origin_seq = c(origin, origin), clock = NULL)
snv_spike <- sim_gt16_nt_diploid(ct_spike, origin_seq = c(origin, origin), clock = NULL)

(plot_alleles(ct_relaxed, snv_relaxed, distance = TRUE) + labs(title = "relaxed")) /
  (plot_alleles(ct_spike, snv_spike, distance = TRUE) + labs(title = "strict + spikes")) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Cells separated by short distances have almost the same genotypes; with spikes, the type 1 cells, whose
divisions add the most distance, differ more from each other than the type 0 cells.

# Error at the tips

The error model of Chen et al. (2022) has two parameters, which act on the sampled tips
(`status == 1`) only, after evolution:

* `epsilon`, **amplification and sequencing error**: the read of an allele shows another nucleotide.
  Each of the six genotypes that differ in one allele is observed with probability `epsilon / 6`
  (times `1 - delta`).
* `delta`, **allelic dropout**: one allele is not amplified, and the other is read twice, so a
  heterozygous site `ab` is observed as `aa` or `bb` (probability `delta / 2` each). Dropout does not
  change homozygous sites, unless it comes with an amplification error of the remaining allele
  (`aa` observed as `bb`, probability `delta * epsilon / 6`).

The marks show the alleles that the error changed, by kind of change: one allele read as another
nucleotide, a heterozygous site read as homozygous for one of its alleles (as after dropout), or both
alleles changed. `plot_alleles(errors = TRUE)` compares the `observed` genotypes of a simulation with its
`true` genotypes:

```{r error, fig.height = 13}
error_settings <- list("epsilon = 0.1" = list(epsilon = 0.1, delta = 0),
                       "delta = 0.3" = list(epsilon = 0, delta = 0.3),
                       "epsilon = 0.1, delta = 0.3" = list(epsilon = 0.1, delta = 0.3))
set.seed(4)
plots <- lapply(names(error_settings), function(name) {
  snv_error <- do.call(sim_gt16_nt_diploid, c(list(tree, origin_seq = c(origin, origin),
                                                   clock = clock_strict(0.15)), error_settings[[name]]))
  plot_alleles(tree, snv_error, errors = TRUE, color = "none") + labs(title = name)
})
wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 1) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Dropout only marks heterozygous sites, and always as het -> hom; amplification and sequencing errors hit
every site, mostly one allele at a time. As for binary sequences, errors are not shared by relatives.

How often each kind occurs depends on the true genotype. On a frozen clock (`clock_strict(0)`), every tip has
the origin genotype; here half of the 2000 sites are homozygous (`AA`) and half heterozygous (`AC`):

```{r error-kinds}
n <- 2000
mixed <- c(strrep("A", n), paste0(strrep("A", n / 2), strrep("C", n / 2)))
tip_kinds <- function(epsilon, delta) {
  out <- sim_gt16_nt_diploid(tree, origin_seq = mixed, clock = clock_strict(0), epsilon = epsilon, delta = delta)
  kinds <- error_kinds(allele_matrices(tree, out, "true"), allele_matrices(tree, out, "observed"))
  site_kind <- ifelse(is.na(kinds$allele1), kinds$allele2, kinds$allele1)  # one kind per site
  site_kind[is.na(site_kind)] <- "none"
  true_genotype <- rep(rep(c("AA", "AC"), each = n / 2), each = nrow(site_kind))
  prop.table(table(true_genotype, factor(site_kind, c("none", names(error_shapes)))), 1)
}
set.seed(5)
lapply(error_settings, function(s) round(tip_kinds(s$epsilon, s$delta), 3))
```

With `epsilon = 0.1`, a homozygous site is observed with one allele changed with probability `epsilon`;
a heterozygous site is also read as homozygous (`epsilon / 3`). With `delta = 0.3`, only heterozygous sites
are affected, with probability `delta`. Both together also turn a few homozygous sites into another
homozygous genotype.

# Choosing parameters

* **`rates`, `pi`**: the nucleotide substitution pattern, e.g. faster transitions, or a skewed base
  composition. Without `origin_seq`, the origin is drawn from `pi`.
* **Clock**: strict, relaxed or with spikes, as in `vignette("simulate_binary")`. For SNVs, distances are per
  genotype site (both alleles); `spike(mean = m / n_sites)` gives about `m` substitutions per division.
* **`epsilon`, `delta`**: the error of single-cell sequencing at the tips. Dropout only shows at heterozygous
  sites, so it matters most for trees with long distances or from a heterozygous origin.

# References
Kozlov, A., Alves, J.M., Stamatakis, A., Posada, D. (2022) CellPhy: accurate and fast probabilistic inference of single-cell phylogenies from scDNA-seq data. Genome Biology, 23(1):37. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-021-02583-w

Chen, K., Moravec, J. C., Gavryushkin, A., Welch, D., & Drummond, A. J. (2022) Accounting for errors in data improves divergence time estimates in single-cell cancer evolution. Molecular Biology and Evolution, 39(8). https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msac143
